transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Welcome back to Green Horizons. Today we're looking at a trend that surprises many people: wildlife is thriving in cities. Foxes in London, coyotes in Chicago, leopards in Mumbai. For a long time, conservationists focused on protecting wilderness. But increasingly, the animals are coming to us.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Take the red fox in Britain. In the 1930s, foxes were almost exclusively found in the countryside. Today, an estimated thirty-three thousand live in urban areas, with the highest densities in cities such as Bristol. They've adapted remarkably well. Foxes eat almost anything, from insects to leftovers, and gardens provide shelter and water. Surveys show that many residents enjoy seeing them, though others complain about noise and overturned bins.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Urban areas can actually be more hospitable than farmland. Modern agriculture has removed hedgerows and used chemical sprays, whereas a city garden might contain flowers, ponds, and unmowed corners. Research in Britain found that bumblebee nests are more common in towns than in farmland, and in some cities hedgehogs, which have declined drastically in the countryside, now survive in larger numbers.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: But there are costs, and not just for people. Animals in cities face dangers such as traffic, which kills millions of creatures every year, and light pollution, which disrupts the behaviour of birds and insects. Studies of urban blackbirds in Europe show that they sing earlier in the day than their rural counterparts, and they begin breeding sooner, possibly because of artificial light and warmer temperatures. Whether these changes are harmful isn't yet known.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Conflict is another issue. In Mumbai, around fifty leopards live in and around a national park surrounded by a city of twenty million. Remarkably, attacks on people are rare, much rarer than one would expect. Researchers believe that this is partly because the leopards feed on stray dogs, and partly because local people have, over generations, learned to live alongside them.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: What can cities do? Experts recommend three measures. First, create wildlife corridors, such as strips of green space connecting parks, so animals can move safely. Second, reduce unnecessary lighting at night. Third, involve residents through citizen science projects, in which people record sightings using an app. These data help scientists understand which species are doing well and which are not.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Of course, urban wildlife isn't a substitute for protecting wild habitats. Many species cannot adapt to cities, and the winners tend to be adaptable generalists. Nevertheless, cities offer an opportunity to reconnect people with nature, and that matters, because people protect what they care about. That's all for this week.
